etymology: Hebrew sheqel, “weight,” from the verb shāqal, “to weigh.” The shekel was originally a unit of weight (approximately 0.4 oz / 11.4 g of silver) before becoming a coin; the Hebrew word means literally that-which-is-weighed.
biblical_def: The shekel is the central unit of weight and currency across the Old Testament, the standard against which other weights and values were measured. Several shekels are distinguished in Scripture. The shekel of the sanctuary (Ex 30:13; 38:24-29) was the temple-standard, used for sacred dues including the half-shekel atonement tax every adult Israelite male paid for the support of the tabernacle service (Ex 30:11-16); twenty gerahs made one shekel of the sanctuary. The king’s shekel (2 Sam 14:26) may have been a different standard for royal weights. The shekel functioned as both weight (for measuring grain, metal, and other commodities) and currency (Abraham’s 400 shekels for the cave of Machpelah, Gen 23:15-16; Joseph sold for 20 shekels of silver, Gen 37:28; Judah’s pledge of a kid, his signet, bracelets, and staff in Gen 38; the bride-price of 50 shekels, Deut 22:29; David’s 50 shekels of silver and an ox-yoke for Araunah’s threshingfloor, 2 Sam 24:24; and the betrayal-price of 30 shekels of silver, Zech 11:12-13 prophetically and Matt 26:15 in fulfillment). The biblical pattern uses the shekel structurally across several theological-and-practical categories. Atonement: every adult Israelite paid a half-shekel for the sanctuary’s service, a token of the ransom by which the soul was kept from being numbered without redemption—a typological anticipation of the full ransom Christ would later pay. Land transactions: significant covenantal land purchases (Abraham’s field, David’s threshingfloor, Jeremiah’s field in chapter 32 as the prophetic sign of God’s coming restoration) are recorded in shekels, anchoring the covenantal land-promise in concrete commerce. Slavery and redemption: the price of a Hebrew slave, the bride-price of a virgin, the value placed on a person dedicated to the LORD (Lev 27)—all are measured in shekels. Betrayal: the 30 shekels of silver Judas received for delivering Christ to the chief priests is the price-tag pre-prophesied in Zechariah 11 of the despised Shepherd, and the fact that it is exactly the price of a slave gored by an ox (Ex 21:32) is the bitterly precise valuation human treachery placed on the Son of God incarnate. The shekel therefore is no merely numismatic curiosity but a structural unit of biblical economics, atonement-doctrine, covenantal land-theology, and the prophetic specification by which the betrayal of Christ is shown to fulfill the Old Testament word.

WEIGHT, n. — That property of bodies by which they tend toward the center of the earth, in proportion to their quantity of matter; a quality measured by the balance and the standard weights.

corruption_summary: The shekel as a biblical unit is corrupted in modern reading chiefly by being treated as a mere historical-numismatic curiosity rather than as a structural unit of biblical atonement-doctrine, covenantal land-theology, and prophetic Christology; recovery requires reading the shekel-weighted transactions as the theological substance they are.
corruption_paragraphs: The contemporary reader, faced with the shekels of Scripture, tends to treat them as ancient currency-curiosities, looking up the modern dollar-equivalent and moving on. The biblical writers used the shekel structurally, and several theological doctrines are tied directly to specific shekel-weighted transactions: the half-shekel of the sanctuary anchors the doctrine of atonement-as-ransom, anticipating the full ransom Christ would pay; Abraham’s 400 shekels for the cave of Machpelah anchor the covenantal land-promise in concrete legal-commercial transaction; David’s 50 shekels for Araunah’s threshingfloor anchor the temple-site in his refusal to offer to God that which cost him nothing; the 30 shekels of Christ’s betrayal anchor the prophetic Zech 11 specification in concrete historical fulfillment. To read past the shekel-figures is to miss the precision with which Scripture has tied its great doctrines to concrete commercial reality.

The supreme case is the 30 shekels of silver paid to Judas. The figure is not arbitrary. Exodus 21:32 specifies 30 shekels as the price of a slave gored by an ox—the basement price of an expendable life. Zechariah 11:12-13 prophetically sets the price at which the despised Shepherd was valued, with the dramatic instruction to cast it unto the potter: a goodly price that I was prised at of them. Matthew 27:9-10 reports the fulfillment in the precise detail: Judas casts the silver in the temple, the priests use it to buy the potter’s field, and the prophet’s word is fulfilled. The price-tag on Christ’s body delivered to His enemies was exactly the price-tag on a slave gored by an ox: the basement valuation of an expendable life, paid by the religious establishment to a faithless friend, fulfilling the prophetic word given centuries before. The contemporary reader who has skipped past 30 shekels of silver as a quaint historical detail has missed one of the most precise prophetic-Christological connections in the entire Bible. Recover the shekel-precision, and recover the doctrinal substance the precision conveys.

etymology: Hebrew kikkār (a round, a circuit; hence a round weight); Greek talanton, “a balance, weight, sum of money.” The largest unit of weight in the ancient world; estimates vary but a talent was approximately 75 lb (34 kg) of silver, equivalent to many years’ wages for a laborer.
biblical_def: The talent was the largest unit of weight and currency in the ancient biblical world—a sum so substantial that it functioned as the standard for major financial transactions, royal tributes, and the metal weights used in the construction of the tabernacle and temple. A single talent of silver was approximately 75 lb (34 kg), worth many years’ wages for an ordinary laborer; a talent of gold was correspondingly more valuable. The construction of the tabernacle used twenty and nine talents and seven hundred and thirty shekels of gold and an hundred talents, and a thousand seven hundred and threescore and fifteen shekels of silver (Ex 38:24-25)—a substantial concentration of precious metals dedicated to the sanctuary. Solomon’s temple construction involved still vaster sums: 100,000 talents of gold and a million talents of silver among the materials David prepared (1 Chr 22:14). The Queen of Sheba brought 120 talents of gold as a gift to Solomon (1 Kgs 10:10). Naaman offered Elisha 10 talents of silver and 6,000 pieces of gold for his cleansing (which Elisha refused; 2 Kgs 5:5). The most famous biblical use of the talent, however, is figurative: Christ’s parable of the talents in Matthew 25:14-30. A man traveling into a far country delivers to his servants his goods: and unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability; and straightway took his journey. The two who put their talents to work doubling them are commended at the master’s return; the one who buried his talent in the earth is rebuked and his talent given to the one with ten. The parable’s lesson is structural to Christian discipleship. The Lord has entrusted to every servant some measure of His gifts (the same word talent has in English come to mean natural gift or aptitude precisely through this parable’s influence); each is to put those gifts to work for the Master’s purposes; faithful stewardship is rewarded and unfaithful neglect is judged; the disparity of original distribution (five, two, one) does not change the principle (each is responsible for the use of what he received). The talent therefore has both a literal-biblical-economic dimension (the largest unit of ancient weight and currency, used for major royal and sacred transactions) and a derived-figurative dimension (the entrusted gifts of the Master, for which every servant gives account at the day of reckoning).

corruption_summary: The talent doctrine is corrupted by the secularized derivation that has retained the figurative sense (natural gift or aptitude) while losing the parable’s underlying claim that the gifts are entrusted by the Master and that every servant must give account at His return—and by the inverse error of the burying-the-talent pattern that the parable explicitly judges.
corruption_paragraphs: The word talent in modern English means natural gift or aptitude—a usage derived directly from Christ’s parable but secularized in the process. Where the parable explicitly grounds the gifts in the Master who entrusted them and the day of reckoning when account must be given, modern usage retains the gift-sense and drops the stewardship-frame: his talents are now spoken of as his own, the products of his nature or upbringing, with no reference to the Giver or to any future accounting. The Christian recovery is the parable’s own framing. The talents are entrusted by the Lord; the servant is steward, not owner; the gifts are given according to his several ability—the Master’s sovereign distribution apportioning differently to different servants; the responsibility is in proportion to what was received; the day of reckoning is coming when each servant will give account of his stewardship. The Christian therefore relates to his abilities, opportunities, time, money, education, and gifts as a steward returning the Master’s deposit with increase—not as an autonomous owner accountable to no one.

The opposite corruption is the buried-talent pattern that the parable explicitly judges. The one-talent servant’s reasoning is a model of how the unfaithful steward justifies his unfruitfulness: I knew thee that thou art an hard man, reaping where thou hast not sown, and gathering where thou hast not strawed: And I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth: lo, there thou hast that is thine. The Master’s response is severe: thou wicked and slothful servant... thou oughtest therefore to have put my money to the exchangers, and then at my coming I should have received mine own with usury. Take therefore the talent from him, and give it unto him which hath ten talents. The lesson is sober. Unfaithful stewardship—the burying of the gift, the failure to put it to work, the rationalization that the Master is too hard to risk loss—is not innocent neglect but actively judged. The contemporary believer who has buried his ministerial gift, his teaching gift, his financial means, his time, his opportunity, his platform, in the soft earth of safety and convenience is the one-talent servant of the parable, and the Master’s reckoning at His return is the same. Recover both ends. Refuse the secularized derivation that severs the gifts from the Giver, and refuse the burying-the-talent pattern that wastes the deposit. The faithful steward puts the talents to work, multiplies them for the Master’s purposes, and at the day of reckoning hears well done, thou good and faithful servant... enter thou into the joy of thy lord.

etymology: Latin cubitum, “elbow”; the unit of measurement based on the length of the human forearm from elbow to tip of middle finger. Hebrew ’ammāh, Greek pēchus. Standardized at approximately 18 inches (45 cm); the “long cubit” (Ezek 40:5) was about 21 inches (53 cm).
biblical_def: The cubit is the standard ancient unit of linear measurement throughout the Bible—the length from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger of a man, approximately 18 inches (45 cm) for the common cubit and approximately 21 inches (53 cm) for the long cubit used in Ezekiel’s temple vision. The cubit governs the measurements of every significant sacred structure described in Scripture. Noah’s ark: the length of the ark shall be three hundred cubits, the breadth of it fifty cubits, and the height of it thirty cubits (Gen 6:15)—a vessel approximately 450 feet long, 75 feet wide, and 45 feet tall, of sufficient capacity to carry the preserved pairs of animal kinds through the flood. The tabernacle’s detailed measurements (Ex 25-27) are given in cubits: the ark of the covenant was two-and-a-half cubits long, one-and-a-half cubits broad, one-and-a-half cubits high; the table of shewbread was two cubits long, one cubit broad, one-and-a-half cubits high; the brazen altar was five cubits square and three cubits high; the tabernacle court was 100 cubits long and 50 cubits broad. Solomon’s temple measurements (1 Kgs 6) are given in cubits: the house was 60 cubits long, 20 cubits broad, and 30 cubits high; the holy of holies was 20 cubits cubed; the porch was 20 cubits broad and 10 cubits deep. Ezekiel’s prophetic temple vision uses the cubit extensively (Ezek 40-48). And the New Jerusalem of Revelation 21:17 is measured: and he measured the wall thereof, an hundred and forty and four cubits, according to the measure of a man, that is, of the angel. The cubit therefore has a deep structural function in biblical narrative: it provides the unit by which God’s sacred architecture is given concrete dimensions, by which the ark of salvation is sized to its purpose, by which the worship-spaces of God’s people are designed, and by which the eschatological architecture of the New Jerusalem is described. Christ Himself uses the cubit figuratively in the Sermon on the Mount: which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature? If ye then be not able to do that thing which is least, why take ye thought for the rest? (Luke 12:25-26). The smallest addition to one’s own life is beyond the worried soul’s power; how then should anxiety be permitted to govern the larger matters?

corruption_summary: The cubit as a biblical unit is corrupted in modern reading chiefly by being treated as a quaint pre-metric historical curiosity rather than as the structural unit by which God’s sacred architecture is concretely designed; recovery requires reading the cubit-measurements with appreciation for the precision and theological substance they carry.
corruption_paragraphs: The contemporary reader, faced with the cubit-measurements of Scripture, tends to convert them quickly to modern equivalents and move on. The biblical writers used the cubit with detailed precision, and the precision is theologically substantive. Noah’s ark’s dimensions (300x50x30 cubits) yield a ratio (10:1.67:1) remarkably similar to that of modern oceangoing vessels designed for stability in heavy seas—the ark was not a fanciful boat-of-the-imagination but a vessel of sound naval architecture. The tabernacle’s measurements describe a portable sanctuary of specific proportions that the LORD Himself commanded—each dimension carrying typological significance the rabbis and church fathers explored across the centuries (the holy of holies as cubical, anticipating the New Jerusalem; the proportions of the ark itself; the relation of the parts to the whole). Solomon’s temple’s measurements show the holy of holies as a perfect cube of 20 cubits—and Revelation 21 ends with the New Jerusalem itself being a perfect cube of 12,000 furlongs, the consummate eschatological echo. The cubit-measurements are therefore not numerical filler but the concrete dimensional substance of God’s sacred architecture across redemptive history.

Christ’s figurative use of the cubit in the Sermon on the Mount is sharply pastoral. Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature? The smallest measurable addition to one’s own being (the cubit being not random but the smallest standardized unit a hearer would clearly visualize) is beyond the worried soul’s power. The argument moves from least to greatest: if the soul cannot add one cubit by anxiety, how then should anxiety be permitted to govern the larger matters of food, clothing, future? The figure depends on the cubit’s being the smallest familiar unit; lose the cubit-vocabulary, and Christ’s argument loses some of its sharpness. Recover the cubit, recover the precision, recover the theological substance the cubit-measurements carry across the canon: the ark of salvation through the flood, the tabernacle and temple of God’s dwelling among His people, the New Jerusalem of the consummate eschatological hope—all concretely measured in the cubit Scripture itself uses.

etymology: From Middle Dutch mite, “a small coin”; renders the Greek lepton, “a thin one,” the smallest copper coin in circulation in NT-era Palestine, worth about 1/128 of a denarius (a single day’s wage for a laborer).
biblical_def: The mite was the smallest copper coin in circulation in the first-century Roman East, rendering the Greek lepton (literally a thin one, the lightest and least-valuable of coins). Two mites made a kodrantes (quadrans, a small Roman copper); 128 quadrantes made a denarius (a single day’s wage); so the mite was worth approximately 1/256 of a day’s wage—the smallest currency unit in actual circulation. The word’s supreme biblical use is the parable-narrative of the widow’s mites in Mark 12:41-44 and Luke 21:1-4. Christ is sitting in the temple opposite the treasury, watching how the people cast in their offerings: and many that were rich cast in much. And there came a certain poor widow, and she threw in two mites, which make a farthing. And he called unto him his disciples, and saith unto them, Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury: For all they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living. The narrative is one of the most theologically dense in the Gospels for its compactness, and several structural points emerge. First, Christ’s assessment overturns the human measurement: the rich gave more in absolute terms, but the widow gave more in proportion-to-what-she-had. The two mites, an objectively trivial sum, are by Christ’s reckoning more than the wealthy donors’ substantial gifts. Second, the measure of biblical giving is therefore not the absolute amount but the proportion-to-what-one-has and the degree-to-which-it-cost. The widow’s two mites cost her everything (all her living); the rich men’s much-larger gifts cost them very little (of their abundance). Third, the narrative is set as Christ’s explicit teaching to His disciples (and he called unto him his disciples): the lesson is meant for the church across the ages, not for the one moment. Fourth, the widow herself is anonymous, unrecognized in her own time, vindicated only by Christ’s seeing-and-naming her gift. The Gospel-narrator’s preserving of her example forever in Scripture is itself part of the lesson: what God sees and values, the world often does not—and the unnoticed widow of the temple-court is honored eternally in the canonical Word, while the wealthy donors of her day are nameless and forgotten. The mite-narrative therefore stands as a structural NT teaching on the nature of biblical giving: not measured in absolute amounts, judged by proportion and cost, valued by what is rendered in faith from what one actually has, seen by the Christ who knows the heart even when men do not see the gift.

corruption_summary: The widow’s mite is corrupted in contemporary use, on one side, by sentimentalized application that has reduced it to a feel-good story about humble giving without the structural challenge to the rich-giving-of-abundance pattern Christ explicitly criticized—and on the other by the prosperity-gospel pattern that asks the widow to give her last living as a seed-faith offering with the promise of a hundredfold return, against the narrative’s actual logic.
corruption_paragraphs: The sentimentalized application has reduced the widow’s mite to a feel-good story about humble giving, often emphasized in stewardship sermons to encourage modest givers without pressing the structural challenge to the comfortable-giving-of-abundance pattern Christ explicitly criticized. The narrative is sharper than the sentimentalization registers. Christ does not merely commend the widow; He criticizes the rich, by name and pattern: they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living. The contrast is not good for her, also good for them; the contrast is between giving-from-overflow (which costs the giver nothing) and giving-of-all-one-has (which costs the giver everything). The implied challenge to the comfortable believer is structural: am I giving from abundance (cheap to me, however much it may be in absolute terms) or in a way that costs me something? The recovery is the recovery of the narrative’s actual logic: biblical giving is measured by what the gift costs the giver, not by the absolute amount placed in the treasury.

The opposite corruption is the prosperity-gospel pattern that has read the widow’s mite as a model for the believer who is to give her last living as a seed-faith offering with the promise of a hundredfold material return. This grossly misreads the narrative. The widow gave her last living; there is no indication that she expected or received material return; she is commended for her sacrifice without any hint that the sacrifice was a transaction for greater material gain. The narrative is a tribute to costly giving without the prosperity-gospel transactional logic, and the contemporary teachers who solicit similar offerings from desperate widows with promises of return-on-investment are repeating a pattern that Christ explicitly criticized elsewhere: woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye devour widows’ houses, and for a pretence make long prayer: therefore ye shall receive the greater damnation (Matt 23:14). Recover both ends. Refuse the sentimentalization that removes the challenge, and refuse the prosperity-gospel reading that converts costly giving into transactional speculation. The widow’s mite stands as Christ’s permanent teaching on the nature of biblical giving: measured by cost-to-the-giver, valued by proportion-to-what-one-has, seen and honored by the Christ who sits opposite the treasury and watches what each soul actually gives.

Biblical giving is measured by cost-to-the-giver and proportion-to-what-one-has, not by the absolute amount placed in the treasury.

Sentimentalization removes the challenge to comfortable abundance-giving; prosperity-gospel reading converts costly sacrifice into transactional speculation; biblical mite-narrative is Christ’s permanent teaching on the nature of true giving.

etymology: From Latin lavare, “to wash”; the bronze basin set between the tabernacle’s door and the brazen altar, at which the priests washed their hands and feet before entering the sanctuary or approaching the altar.
biblical_def: The laver was the bronze basin set in the court of the tabernacle (later, in Solomon’s temple, a vastly larger bronze basin called the molten sea on twelve oxen, 1 Kgs 7:23-26) at which the priests washed their hands and feet before entering the sanctuary or approaching the altar to minister. Exodus 30:17-21 prescribes the laver: thou shalt also make a laver of brass, and his foot also of brass, to wash withal: and thou shalt put it between the tabernacle of the congregation and the altar, and thou shalt put water therein. For Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet thereat: When they go into the tabernacle of the congregation, they shall wash with water, that they die not; or when they come near to the altar to minister, to burn offering made by fire unto the LORD: So they shall wash their hands and their feet, that they die not: and it shall be a statute for ever to them, even to him and to his seed throughout their generations. Several structural features mark the laver’s theological function. First, it stood between the altar and the sanctuary, geographically and ritually—the priest who had come past the altar of sacrifice now stood at the laver before proceeding further into the holy place. Atonement (the altar) preceded cleansing (the laver) preceded ministry (the sanctuary). Second, the failure to wash carried capital sanction: that they die not, repeated twice in the passage. The laver’s ritual was not optional but binding under death. Third, the laver was made from the looking-glasses of the women who served at the door of the tabernacle (Ex 38:8)—a detail of detailed significance: the mirrors by which the women had checked their outward appearance became the basin in which the priests examined themselves before approaching the LORD. Fourth, the laver had its New Covenant fulfillment in the cleansing the saint receives through the Word and the washing of regeneration. Ephesians 5:25-27: husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it; That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word, That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish. Titus 3:5: not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost. Hebrews 10:22: let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water. The laver therefore typifies the ongoing cleansing the saint receives at the throne of grace, by which he is fitted for the priestly service to which he has been called: regeneration washes him once; the Word and the Spirit continue to wash him daily; the discipline of self-examination at the laver fits him for the worship and service in which he approaches the LORD.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LAVER as a vessel for washing; a bronze basin in the tabernacle and temple at which the priests washed before entering the sanctuary or approaching the altar; fulfilled in the New Covenant by the washing of regeneration and the daily cleansing by the Word.

WASH, v.t. — To cleanse by means of water and rubbing; to remove dirt or filth by water. In scripture, to cleanse from sin by the blood of Christ, the washing of regeneration, and the cleansing of the Word.

corruption_summary: The laver-doctrine is corrupted, on one side, by the loss of the laver-typology in much contemporary preaching that has stopped tracing the Old Testament types to their New Testament fulfillments—and on the other by the sacramental over-reading that has identified the laver’s typological fulfillment exclusively with baptismal regeneration, against the broader NT teaching of the Word and the Spirit’s ongoing cleansing through Word and prayer.
corruption_paragraphs: The loss of the laver-typology is a wider symptom of the general loss of typological reading in much contemporary preaching. The Old Testament types—the tabernacle furnishings, the priestly garments, the sacrifices, the feasts, the persons of the patriarchs and judges—are no longer regularly traced to their New Testament fulfillments. The result is a Bible whose Old Testament is preached in isolation from its Christological substance and whose New Testament loses much of the depth the Old Testament types supply. The laver is one specific case: a basin between altar and sanctuary, prescribed under penalty of death, whose New Covenant fulfillment is the cleansing by the Word and the washing of regeneration that fits the saint for priestly service. To preach the laver as ancient cultic detail without tracing its typological substance is to miss what the Spirit who inspired both testaments was doing in the structure He gave.

The opposite corruption is the sacramental over-reading that has identified the laver’s typological fulfillment exclusively with baptismal regeneration—treating water-baptism as the once-for-all answer to the laver, with no acknowledgment of the ongoing cleansing by the Word the New Testament also teaches. Eph 5:26 specifies that Christ sanctifies and cleanses the church with the washing of water by the word: the Word itself is the cleansing means, applied across the believer’s lifetime. The laver-typology therefore points not only to the once-for-all regenerating washing at conversion but also to the ongoing cleansing by which the saint, daily approaching the throne of grace, is fitted for the worship and service in which he stands. Recover both ends. Refuse the loss of typology that abandons the laver-doctrine altogether, and refuse the sacramental over-reading that confines its fulfillment to baptism alone. The biblical laver typifies both the regenerating washing at conversion (Tit 3:5) and the ongoing Word-and-Spirit cleansing across the Christian life (Eph 5:26), by which the priestly saint is daily fitted for the holy service to which he has been called.

etymology: Shew (archaic for show) + bread; renders the Hebrew lechem ha-pānīm, literally bread of the face or bread of the presence; the twelve loaves placed weekly on the gold table in the holy place of the tabernacle and temple.
biblical_def: The shewbread (literally bread of the face/presence) was the twelve loaves placed weekly on the gold table in the holy place of the tabernacle, and subsequently of the temple, throughout the Old Testament period. Leviticus 24:5-9 prescribes the ritual: and thou shalt take fine flour, and bake twelve cakes thereof: two tenth deals shall be in one cake. And thou shalt set them in two rows, six on a row, upon the pure table before the LORD. And thou shalt put pure frankincense upon each row, that it may be on the bread for a memorial, even an offering made by fire unto the LORD. Every sabbath he shall set it in order before the LORD continually, being taken from the children of Israel by an everlasting covenant. And it shall be Aaron’s and his sons’; and they shall eat it in the holy place: for it is most holy unto him of the offerings of the LORD made by fire by a perpetual statute. Several structural features mark the doctrine. First, the twelve loaves represented the twelve tribes of Israel—the whole covenant people set before the LORD perpetually as the bread of His presence. Second, the loaves were placed in the holy place, the second of the tabernacle’s three zones (the court, the holy place, the holy of holies); they stood opposite the gold lampstand, with the altar of incense between the table and the veil. Third, the loaves were replaced weekly on the Sabbath; the old loaves were eaten by the priests in the holy place—a perpetual covenantal communion-meal between the priests representing the people and the LORD before whom the bread was set. Fourth, the bread was continually before the LORD—there was never a moment in tabernacle or temple history when the bread of the presence was absent from the gold table. The shewbread therefore has several theological functions. Liturgically: a perpetual memorial of the covenant relationship between the LORD and His people, with the people’s representative-bread always before His face. Typologically: pointing toward the Christ who would Himself be the bread of life, given to the church as the perpetual sustenance of the people of God. Ecclesially: anticipating the Lord’s Supper at which the bread of the Lord’s body is given to the saints as the covenantal meal of the new covenant. Christ’s reference to the shewbread in Matthew 12:3-4 (defending His disciples’ eating of corn on the Sabbath by appealing to David’s eating of the shewbread in 1 Sam 21) shows His use of the shewbread-history for pastoral and theological argument: the ceremonial law’s details serve God’s purpose for His people; the Sabbath itself is for man and not man for the Sabbath; the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath. The shewbread-typology continues into the New Covenant: the bread of His presence becomes the bread of the Lord’s table, given to His new covenant people as the perpetual memorial of His body broken for them and the sign of their covenantal communion with Him.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SHEWBREAD as the bread of the presence; twelve loaves placed every sabbath on the holy table in the tabernacle and temple, representing the twelve tribes of Israel and serving as a perpetual covenantal memorial.
webster_full: SHEWBREAD, n. — Among the Jews, bread of exhibition; the twelve loaves of bread which the priest of the week placed before the Lord on the golden table in the sanctuary. They were renewed every Sabbath, and only the priests were permitted to eat them.
SHEW, v.t. — (Archaic for SHOW.) To exhibit or present to the view of another; to set before.

corruption_summary: The shewbread-doctrine is corrupted in much contemporary preaching by the general loss of typological reading that no longer traces the tabernacle furnishings to their Christological and ecclesial fulfillments—and by the inverse over-allegorization in some traditions that extracts arbitrary spiritual meaning from every architectural detail without grounding in the typological-Christological substance the New Testament itself authorizes.
corruption_paragraphs: The general loss of typological reading in much contemporary preaching is the broader corruption that affects the shewbread along with other tabernacle furnishings. The twelve loaves of presence-bread are taught (where they are taught at all) as ancient cultic detail without serious tracing to their Christological substance: Christ as the bread of life, the church as the new covenant people whose representative-bread is now the bread of the Lord’s table, the Sabbath-renewal of the shewbread anticipating the Sabbath-rest of the new covenant. The recovery is the recovery of typological reading itself, with the New Testament’s own treatment as the controlling guide. Christ’s appeal to the shewbread in defense of His Sabbath ministry (Matt 12:3-4) authorizes typological-pastoral use of the detail; John 6’s great I am the bread of life discourse provides the Christological substance the shewbread-typology was always pointing toward; the Lord’s table provides the new covenant’s perpetual covenantal meal that the shewbread was forever anticipating.

The opposite corruption is the over-allegorization in some traditions that extracts arbitrary spiritual meaning from every architectural detail (the precise dimensions of the table, the specific number of horns on the altar, the colors of the curtains) without grounding in the typological-Christological substance the New Testament itself authorizes. Tabernacle-allegorizing of this kind has, in some preaching traditions, produced sermons of impressive ingenuity and dubious doctrinal weight; the imagined meanings often have no biblical basis and shift from preacher to preacher. The biblical balance is precise. Typological reading is authorized where the NT itself does it (Christ as bread of life for the shewbread; Christ as light of the world for the lampstand; Christ as Mediator for the veil); typological inference is appropriate where it is grounded in the NT’s own pattern; bare allegorization of details the NT does not address is to be avoided. The shewbread-typology, well-anchored in John 6 and the Lord’s table, stands; the over-allegorizations of impressive-but-ungrounded inventiveness do not. The recovery of disciplined typological reading is the path between the loss of typology and its over-extension.

etymology: Latin spica nardi, “spike of nard”; a costly aromatic ointment derived from the spikenard plant (Nardostachys jatamansi) native to the Himalayas, expensive to import to Palestine, used in luxury anointings.
biblical_def: Spikenard is the costly aromatic ointment derived from the spikenard plant (Nardostachys jatamansi) native to the Himalayas, imported at great expense to the ancient Mediterranean world and used in luxury anointings. The substance is referenced twice in the Song of Solomon as part of the bride’s and the bridegroom’s mutual delights: while the king sitteth at his table, my spikenard sendeth forth the smell thereof (Song 1:12); spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense; myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices (Song 4:14). But its supreme biblical appearance is in the anointing-of-Christ narratives of Mark 14:3-9 and John 12:1-8. Mary of Bethany breaks an alabaster box of spikenard very precious and pours it on Christ’s head (Mark) or anoints His feet and wipes them with her hair (John); the disciples—and notably Judas, who would shortly betray Him for thirty pieces of silver—object that this ointment might have been sold for more than three hundred pence (denarii), and given to the poor. Christ’s response is one of the most theologically dense passages in the Gospels: let her alone; against the day of my burying hath she kept this. For the poor always ye have with you; but me ye have not always... Verily I say unto you, Wheresoever this gospel shall be preached throughout the whole world, this also that she hath done shall be spoken of for a memorial of her. Several structural points emerge from the narrative. First, the cost: three hundred denarii is approximately a year’s wages for a laborer; Mary’s gift is genuinely costly, not symbolic-poverty. Second, the timing: Mary alone among Christ’s associates grasps that He is about to die, and her anointing is, in His own words, against the day of my burying—a prophetic act of preparation that the male disciples, who had heard Christ predict His death repeatedly, had not understood. Third, the criticism: Judas’s objection (with the cover of concern for the poor masking his own thievery, John 12:6) is the precise type of pious-sounding rationalization that has always been deployed against costly devotion to Christ. Fourth, Christ’s vindication: Mary’s extravagance, criticized in its moment, is canonized in the Gospels as the perpetual memorial of devotion wheresoever this gospel shall be preached throughout the whole world—and the Gospel narrators have preserved the memorial as Christ commanded. The spikenard-narrative therefore stands as Scripture’s great teaching on costly devotion to Christ: real cost, prophetic insight, vindicated by Christ over the criticism of the merely-practical, canonized for the encouragement of every subsequent saint who has been criticized for similarly extravagant devotion to the Lord who deserves it.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SPIKENARD as a plant of the genus Nardostachys, and the costly aromatic ointment derived from it; in scripture, the precious ointment Mary of Bethany poured on Christ in anticipation of His burial (John 12:3), commended by Christ over the criticism of His disciples and canonized as the perpetual memorial of costly devotion.
webster_full: SPIKENARD, n. — 1. A plant of the genus Nardostachys, growing in the mountains of India. 2. An aromatic essential oil obtained from this plant, used as a perfume and as a costly anointing oil. Mary took a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly (John 12:3).
NARD, n. — (See SPIKENARD.) An aromatic plant and the costly ointment derived from it.

corruption_summary: The spikenard-narrative is corrupted, in contemporary application, by the Judas-style rationalization that mistakes mere practicality for biblical wisdom and criticizes costly devotion to Christ as wasteful—and by the inverse sentimentalization that has lost the prophetic and costly substance of Mary’s act and treats it as a feel-good story without the structural challenge to comfortable Christianity.
corruption_paragraphs: The Judas-style rationalization is the precise pattern Christ rebuked at the dinner in Bethany, and the pattern recurs in every age. Costly devotion to Christ—the disproportionate giving to gospel-mission, the sacrificial generosity that puts the kingdom first, the extravagant offering that the merely-practical would call wasteful—is met with the pious-sounding objection: this might have been better used elsewhere; the cost is excessive; surely something more modest would have served as well. Judas’s motive in John 12 is exposed as theft hidden behind concern for the poor; the modern Judas-style criticism may have purer motives, but it deploys the same logic against the same kind of devotion. Christ’s response in the narrative is the standing answer: let her alone... the poor always ye have with you; but me ye have not always. Devotion to Christ has its own logic, and the criticism of the merely-practical is to be answered in His name. The recovery is the freedom to give extravagantly to Christ where the heart is moved to do so, with the assurance that what looks wasteful to the practical is canonized by Christ as memorial-worthy.

The opposite contemporary corruption is the sentimentalization that has lost the prophetic and costly substance of Mary’s act and treats it as a feel-good story without the structural challenge to comfortable Christianity. Mary’s gift cost a year’s wages; she grasped Christ’s imminent death when the male disciples did not; her act was prophetic insight expressed in extravagant devotion. The sentimentalized version that turns Mary into a generic figure of doing a sweet thing for Jesus misses the specific costliness, the specific prophetic insight, and the specific challenge the narrative poses to those who would never give a year’s wages to anything that did not have an obvious return-on-investment. Recover both ends. Refuse the Judas-style rationalization that criticizes costly devotion as wasteful, and refuse the sentimentalization that strips the narrative of its prophetic and costly substance. The biblical spikenard-narrative is Christ’s perpetual encouragement to every saint who, like Mary, is moved to costly devotion to Him, against the criticism of those who do not understand what only the Spirit teaches the loving heart to grasp.

etymology: Middle English conig from Old French conin, from Latin cuniculus, “rabbit.” In the KJV, however, the word translates the Hebrew shāphān, which most modern scholars identify as the rock hyrax (Procavia capensis), a small mammal of Sinai and the Holy Land, not the European rabbit.
biblical_def: The coney in the KJV is the small mammal called in modern English the rock hyrax—a furry, rodent-looking creature of approximately rabbit size that lives in colonies among the rocks of Sinai, Arabia, and the Holy Land. The KJV translators rendered the Hebrew shāphān as coney (a Middle English word that originally meant rabbit) because no European reader of the early 1600s would have known the rock hyrax by name; the rabbit was the closest familiar approximation. The coney appears four times in the Old Testament. Twice in the lists of unclean animals: and the coney, because he cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof; he is unclean unto you (Lev 11:5; cf. Deut 14:7). The coney’s ruminant-style chewing motion (it chews and re-chews its food in a way that resembles cud-chewing without being technically the same process) and its lack of cloven hoofs put it in the unclean category of animals Israel was forbidden to eat. Twice in the wisdom literature, however, the coney appears in a different register: the high hills are a refuge for the wild goats; and the rocks for the conies (Ps 104:18); and most strikingly, the conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks (Prov 30:26). The Proverbs reference is the one with the deepest pastoral application. The coney is named as one of four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise (Prov 30:24-28): the ants, the conies, the locusts, and the spider. The coney’s wisdom is precisely its self-knowledge: it is a feeble creature, defenseless against predators, with no speed, no claws, no horns—and it has wisely chosen to dwell in the rocks where its weakness is compensated by the inaccessibility of its refuge. The application to the saint is direct. The saint is a feeble creature (Ps 103:14: he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust), defenseless in himself against the spiritual predators arrayed against him, with no native strength against the powers of darkness. Like the coney, he is wise to make his house in the Rock—the Rock who is Christ (1 Cor 10:4), the Rock of his salvation (Deut 32:15; 2 Sam 22:47; Ps 18:46), the Rock higher than I (Ps 61:2). The feeble folk who dwell in the Rock is the picture of every saint in every generation: weak in himself, strong in his refuge, made wise by his honest assessment of his own weakness and his deliberate flight to the Rock that is stronger than every assault.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CONEY as a rabbit; in the KJV, however, used for the Hebrew shāphān, which is the rock hyrax of Sinai and the Holy Land; biblically significant as one of Proverbs 30’s four wise feeble things, the feeble folk who make their houses in the rocks.
webster_full: CONEY, n. — A rabbit; in scripture (KJV), the rock hyrax (shāphān), a small mammal of the Holy Land. The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks (Prov 30:26).

ROCK, n. — A large mass of stony matter, usually compounded of two or more simple minerals. In scripture, often used as a figure of the LORD as the firm support and refuge of His people (Deut 32:4; Ps 18:2; 1 Cor 10:4).
scriptures: Proverbs 30:24-26

There be four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise: The ants are a people not strong, yet they prepare their meat in the summer; The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks.
Psalm 104:18
The high hills are a refuge for the wild goats; and the rocks for the conies.
Leviticus 11:5
And the coney, because he cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof; he is unclean unto you.
Psalm 18:2
The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower.
corruption_summary: The coney-doctrine is corrupted chiefly by being overlooked altogether—a minor zoological detail in the dietary laws and a passing wisdom-literature reference, often skipped in contemporary preaching—and by the loss of the pastoral application of Proverbs 30:26 to the saint as the feeble folk wisely dwelling in the Rock that is Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The coney is one of many small biblical creatures (along with the spider, the locust, the ant) that contemporary preaching tends to skip past as zoological curiosities of a vanished agrarian world. Proverbs 30’s four wise feeble things are not, however, mere natural-history. They are pastoral wisdom embodied in observation: the ants’ preparation in summer for the want of winter (a parable of foresight and diligence); the conies’ choosing-of-rocks for their refuge (a parable of honest self-assessment and wise flight to a stronger refuge); the locusts’ ordered swarming without a king (a parable of cooperative unity); the spider’s skilled work in places of human power (a parable of patient skill reaching places the powerful cannot bar). Each yields pastoral substance the careful reader is meant to draw. The recovery is the recovery of the Proverbs-style observation: the natural world is full of parables the Spirit-trained eye sees, and the wisdom literature trains the saint to look and see and learn.

The supreme pastoral application of the coney specifically is to the doctrine of the saint as the feeble folk who wisely dwells in the Rock. The Bible knows no flattering doctrine of human native strength; it is candid about the creaturely weakness, the indwelling sin, the spiritual powers arrayed against the believer. The coney’s wisdom is the saint’s wisdom: honest assessment of one’s own feebleness, deliberate flight to the Rock that is Christ. The saint who has not assessed his own weakness has not yet learned what the coney teaches; the saint who has assessed his weakness and has not yet fled to the Rock is in the unguarded condition of the feeble creature exposed in the open. The recovery is the recovery of the picture: see your weakness honestly, see Christ as the Rock that is stronger than every assault, dwell in Him, find in Him the refuge no native strength could provide. The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks—a pastoral picture worth thirty volumes of self-help on developing native strength.
roots_summary: Hebrew shāphān (the rock hyrax; rendered coney in the KJV); appears in the dietary laws as unclean (Lev 11:5; Deut 14:7) and in the wisdom literature as the feeble folk who wisely dwells in the rocks (Ps 104:18; Prov 30:26)—the pastoral picture of the saint dwelling in the Rock that is Christ.

Greek petra (G4073) — rock (the great NT word for the Christ-Rock; 1 Cor 10:4; Matt 16:18).
Hebrew tsur (H6697) — rock, cliff (the OT word for the LORD as Rock; Deut 32:4; Ps 18:2).
Hebrew sela‘ (H5553) — cliff, rock (used for the conies’ refuge in Ps 104:18).
usage: The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks—Proverbs 30:26’s pastoral picture of the saint dwelling in Christ the Rock.
The coney’s wisdom is precisely its honest self-assessment of weakness paired with its deliberate flight to a stronger refuge.
Contemporary preaching tends to skip the small biblical creatures as zoological curiosities; the wisdom literature treats them as pastoral parables the Spirit-trained eye learns to see.

etymology: Greek onyx, “fingernail, claw”; named for the stone’s color resembling a fingernail. Hebrew shoham, identified with onyx (a variety of chalcedony with parallel banded colors, often black-and-white, brown-and-white, or red-and-white); used in the high priest’s breastplate and ephod.
biblical_def: Onyx (Hebrew shoham) is one of the precious stones identified by Scripture with particular theological-priestly significance, used in the high priest’s vestments to represent the twelve tribes of Israel before the LORD perpetually. Exodus 28:9-12 prescribes the use: and thou shalt take two onyx stones, and grave on them the names of the children of Israel: Six of their names on one stone, and the other six names of the rest on the other stone, according to their birth. With the work of an engraver in stone, like the engravings of a signet, shalt thou engrave the two stones with the names of the children of Israel: thou shalt make them to be set in ouches of gold. And thou shalt put the two stones upon the shoulders of the ephod for stones of memorial unto the children of Israel: and Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD upon his two shoulders for a memorial. Several structural features mark the doctrine. First, the engraving: the names of the twelve tribes are graven into the stones with the permanence of signet-engraving, an indelible marking. Second, the location: the stones are set on the shoulders of the ephod—the place of bearing burdens, the structural-supporting region of the body. The high priest carries the names of the twelve tribes on his shoulders, perpetually bearing them as he ministers before the LORD. Third, the function: for a memorial—the stones cause the names to be perpetually remembered before the LORD’s face as the high priest stands in His presence. The onyx stones are therefore a covenantal-priestly device by which the people of God are kept perpetually before His face through their representative who bears their names on his shoulders into the holy place. The typological fulfillment in Christ is unmistakable. Christ as our Great High Priest perpetually bears the names of His people on His shoulders into the presence of the Father: seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession (Heb 4:14); wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them (Heb 7:25); for Christ is not entered into the holy places made with hands, which are the figures of the true; but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us (Heb 9:24). The names of the redeemed are graven into the very being of the great High Priest who bears them perpetually before the Father; the Aaronic onyx stones were the shadow whose substance is Christ Himself bearing His people before God in His unceasing intercession. Onyx also appears at the beginning and the end of Scripture: in the land of Havilah at creation (Gen 2:12, and the gold of that land is good: there is bdellium and the onyx stone), and among the foundation stones of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20). The stone traverses the canonical arc from creation to consummation, from Eden’s good land to the city of God.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ONYX as a semi-pellucid gem with various colors of veins, especially black and white in parallel layers; in scripture, the stone used for the two engraved stones on the shoulders of the high priest’s ephod, bearing the names of the twelve tribes for a perpetual memorial before the LORD.
webster_full: ONYX, n. — A semi-pellucid gem, with variously colored veins, often black and white in parallel layers; a variety of chalcedony. In scripture, used in the high priest’s ephod (Ex 28:9-12) and among the foundation stones of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20).
EPHOD, n. — A piece of dress worn by the Jewish priests; the outer garment of the high priest, on the shoulders of which the onyx stones were set.

corruption_summary: The onyx-doctrine is corrupted in much contemporary preaching by the general loss of typological reading that no longer traces the high priest’s ephod-stones to their Christological fulfillment in the great High Priest who perpetually bears His people’s names before the Father—and by the inverse over-allegorization that extracts arbitrary spiritual meaning from each gemstone without the typological-Christological grounding the NT itself provides.
corruption_paragraphs: The general loss of typological reading affects the onyx-doctrine as it does the broader tabernacle-and-priesthood typology. The two engraved onyx stones on the high priest’s shoulders are taught (where they are taught at all) as ancient priestly detail without serious tracing to their fulfillment in Christ the Great High Priest who perpetually bears His people’s names before the Father. The recovery is the recovery of the typology, with Hebrews 7–10’s sustained Christ-as-high-priest argument providing the controlling framework. Christ is the substance of which the Aaronic priesthood was the shadow; the onyx stones bearing the names of the twelve tribes typify the substantive reality that Christ Himself carries the names of His redeemed people perpetually into the presence of God in His unceasing intercession. The pastoral application is direct and tender: the saint’s name is borne on the shoulders of his great High Priest perpetually before the Father; he is never forgotten, never absent from the holy place, never out of the High Priest’s remembrance. The recovery of the doctrine is the recovery of one of the deepest pastoral consolations Scripture supplies.

The opposite corruption is the over-allegorization that extracts arbitrary spiritual meaning from each gemstone (the onyx specifically signifying something the text does not specify, with imagined correspondences between particular stones and particular tribes, particular virtues, particular events of salvation history) without the typological-Christological grounding the NT itself authorizes. Tabernacle-allegorizing of this kind, when it loses its biblical anchor, becomes preacher-invention rather than disciplined typological reading. The biblical pattern is precise. Typological reading is appropriate where the NT itself does it (Christ as Great High Priest is the controlling framework for tabernacle typology); typological inference is appropriate where it is grounded in the NT’s own pattern; bare allegorization of details the NT does not address is to be avoided. The onyx-typology, well-anchored in the Hebrews high-priest doctrine, stands; the imagined gemstone-correspondences of impressive-but-ungrounded preaching do not. The recovery is disciplined typological reading: rich enough to draw out the pastoral substance, restrained enough not to invent meaning the Spirit did not put there.
roots_summary: Greek onyx (fingernail, claw—named for the stone’s color); Hebrew shoham; the precious stone used for the two engraved stones on the shoulders of the high priest’s ephod, bearing the names of the twelve tribes for a perpetual memorial before the LORD; typologically fulfilled in Christ the Great High Priest who bears His people’s names perpetually before the Father.
roots_lines: Greek onyx — fingernail, claw (the etymological source of English onyx, from the stone’s color).
Greek sardonyx (G4557) — sardonyx (Rev 21:20; the fifth foundation stone of the New Jerusalem).
Hebrew ephod (H646) — ephod (the high priest’s vestment on whose shoulders the onyx stones were set).
usage: The two onyx stones on the high priest’s shoulders bore the names of the twelve tribes for a perpetual memorial before the LORD.
Christ as our Great High Priest perpetually bears the names of His people on His shoulders into the presence of the Father—Heb 7:25, ever living to make intercession.
The saint’s pastoral consolation: his name is borne on the shoulders of his great High Priest perpetually before the Father; he is never forgotten, never absent from the holy place.

etymology: Greek psaltērion, from psallō, “to pluck (a string)”; the stringed instrument plucked with the fingers in accompaniment to the singing of psalms. Cognate of psalmos (psalm) and psaltēs (a singer with the psaltery).
biblical_def: The psaltery is one of the chief stringed instruments of Old Testament worship—a harp-like instrument with strings plucked by the fingers, used extensively in temple worship, royal worship, and the personal devotion of David and other psalmists. The instrument appears across the Old Testament in worship contexts. David appoints the Levites for musical service: moreover David and the captains of the host separated to the service of the sons of Asaph, and of Heman, and of Jeduthun, who should prophesy with harps, with psalteries, and with cymbals (1 Chr 25:1); these were the musicians of the tabernacle and subsequently the temple. The dedication of Solomon’s temple involved the Levites which were the singers, all of them of Asaph, of Heman, of Jeduthun, with their sons and their brethren, being arrayed in white linen, having cymbals and psalteries and harps, stood at the east end of the altar, and with them an hundred and twenty priests sounding with trumpets (2 Chr 5:12). The Psalter is saturated with calls to praise with the psaltery: praise the LORD with harp: sing unto him with the psaltery and an instrument of ten strings (Ps 33:2); praise him with the psaltery and harp (Ps 150:3); I will praise thee with the psaltery, even thy truth, O my God: unto thee will I sing with the harp, O thou Holy One of Israel (Ps 71:22). The instrument was so closely tied to the singing of psalms that its name and the name of the song-collection (Psalter, the book of Psalms) share the same Greek etymological root—psallō, to pluck a string. Several structural features mark the doctrine of biblical musical worship that the psaltery helps anchor. First, instrumental music was integral to Old Testament temple worship—not a concession to weakness but a divinely-appointed component of corporate praise. Second, the Levitical musicians were ordained for the work, qualified by training and gift, set apart for the service: not casual volunteers but recognized officers. Third, the psaltery (with the harp, cymbals, and trumpets) served the singing of the inspired psalms rather than replacing it; the music supported the Word, not the reverse. Fourth, the New Testament continues the imagery (the elders in heaven hold harps in Rev 5:8; 14:2; 15:2) even while Christian worship in the apostolic period was apparently simpler in instrumentation than the temple service had been. The post-apostolic and Reformation traditions have varied in their use of instruments in worship, with some traditions retaining a cappella psalm-singing as closer to the apostolic pattern and others incorporating instruments as an aid to corporate praise. The psaltery itself, as a specific instrument, is no longer in common use; but the doctrine of musical worship that the psaltery helped anchor in OT worship continues to inform Christian thought about how the church praises her God.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PSALTERY as an instrument of music used by the ancient Hebrews, the form of which is not now known; in scripture, a stringed instrument plucked with the fingers, used extensively in temple worship and called for repeatedly in the Psalter.
webster_full: PSALTERY, n. — An instrument of music used by the ancient Hebrews, the form of which is not now known. The instrument was plucked with the fingers; the name is from the Greek psallō, to pluck. Praise him with the psaltery and harp (Ps 150:3).
PSALM, n. — A sacred song or hymn; especially, one of the inspired songs of the Hebrew Bible, the book of Psalms.

Praise the LORD with harp: sing unto him with the psaltery and an instrument of ten strings.
Psalm 150:3
Praise him with the sound of the trumpet: praise him with the psaltery and harp.
1 Chronicles 25:1
Moreover David and the captains of the host separated to the service of the sons of Asaph, and of Heman, and of Jeduthun, who should prophesy with harps, with psalteries, and with cymbals.

corruption_summary: The psaltery as a specific instrument has dropped from contemporary use, but the doctrine of biblical musical worship it helped anchor is corrupted by two opposite contemporary patterns: the entertainment-driven worship that has subordinated the Word to musical performance, and the inverse minimalism that has so reduced the music as to lose the rich biblical pattern of God-glorifying instrumental praise the Psalter calls for.
corruption_paragraphs: The entertainment-driven worship of much contemporary evangelicalism has subordinated the Word to musical performance, inverting the biblical relationship in which the music served the singing of inspired psalms and the proclamation of the Word. The contemporary pattern often has the worship-band leading, the music swelling, the lighting engineered, and the sermon as one component (sometimes shortened) in a service whose dominant note is musical-experiential rather than Word-centered. The biblical pattern—both Old Testament and apostolic—sets the Word at the center, with music supporting and adorning the singing of psalms and hymns rather than competing with or eclipsing the Word. Recover the doctrine, and the music recovers its biblical place: rich, full-throated, instrumentally accompanied corporate praise that serves the Word and the gospel rather than substituting for them.

The opposite corruption is the inverse minimalism that has so reduced the music as to lose the rich biblical pattern of God-glorifying instrumental praise the Psalter calls for. Some traditions, especially in their anti-entertainment reactions, have practically eliminated musical instruments and reduced the music to spare, plain, unaccompanied singing that, while sincere, does not reach the biblical fullness of Psalm 150’s call to praise the LORD with trumpet, psaltery, harp, timbrel, dance, stringed instruments, organs, loud cymbals, and high-sounding cymbals. The Psalter’s vision of corporate praise is rich and full-instrumented; the contemporary minimalist reaction can sometimes drift toward an under-instrumented practice that the Bible itself does not warrant. Recover both ends. Refuse the entertainment-driven inversion that subordinates the Word to musical performance, and refuse the minimalist reduction that loses the rich biblical pattern of instrumental praise. The biblical pattern is full-throated, instrumentally adorned, gospel-saturated corporate praise that serves the Word and exalts the God to whom the music is offered.
roots_summary: Greek psaltērion (from psallō, to pluck a string); Hebrew nēbel (psaltery, harp); the stringed instrument of Old Testament temple worship, called for repeatedly in the Psalter (Ps 33:2; 71:22; 81:2; 92:3; 108:2; 144:9; 150:3) and used in the appointed Levitical musical service.
roots_lines: Hebrew nēbel (H5035) — psaltery, harp, lute (the OT term; 27 OT uses).
Greek psaltērion — psaltery (the LXX translation of nēbel).
Greek psallō (G5567) — to pluck (a string); to sing psalms (Rom 15:9; 1 Cor 14:15; Eph 5:19; Jas 5:13).
Greek psalmos (G5568) — a psalm (the sung composition; 7 NT uses, all in worship contexts).
usage: Praise him with the psaltery and harp—Ps 150 calls for full-instrumented corporate praise of the LORD.
The Levitical musicians were ordained for the work, qualified by training and gift, set apart for the service—not casual volunteers but recognized officers of temple worship.

The biblical pattern sets music as servant of the Word; entertainment-driven worship inverts the relation, minimalist reduction loses the rich instrumental fullness Psalm 150 calls for; recovery is full-throated, Word-serving, gospel-saturated corporate praise.
